bridges.description: Show that the Biblical Trinitarian God exists rather than merely that some explanation is missing.
Connect universal logical norms to a transcendent divine mind.
Connect the universe’s finite beginning to a timeless personal choice.
Ground objective moral truth in God rather than preference.
Identify and defend the attributes and revelation of the specific Biblical God.
Reconcile suffering and unanswered prayer with the existence and character of God.
Show that withholding belief remains justified unless the additional God claim receives adequate support.
Explain logical concepts without inferring independently existing transcendent objects.
Challenge the extension of ordinary causation beyond spacetime and preserve natural alternatives.
Test whether the defended divine attributes can jointly describe a possible personal being.
Compare claimed divine evidence with observable effects and rival explanations.
Ground moral deliberation and altruism in harm, well-being, and evolved social capacities.
Test whether scripture and religious agreement reliably identify the Biblical God.

sections.title: Burden and public evidence
sections.rationale: Frames the exact motion, the asymmetry between an existence claim and critical nonbelief, and what could count as public support.

sections.title: Logic and intelligibility
sections.rationale: Covers the central dispute over whether universal logical norms require a transcendent mind.

sections.title: Cosmology and causation
sections.rationale: Covers the finite-universe, personal-cause, fine-tuning, and natural-alternative arguments.

sections.title: Divine coherence
sections.rationale: Tests whether omniscience, free decision, personhood, and the parties’ freedom distinctions can jointly describe the proposed God.

sections.title: Revelation and divine authority
sections.rationale: Examines how the Biblical God is identified through attributes, scripture, experience, agreement, and an account of morality grounded in divine nature.

sections.title: Morality and altruism
sections.rationale: Compares divine grounding with harm-based ethics and natural accounts of costly helping.

sections.title: Suffering and prayer
sections.rationale: Examines evil, healing, prayer, providence, and the scope of conclusions drawn from suffering.

moves.speaker: Matt Slick
moves.claim: Slick argues that the universe’s finite beginning requires a personal rather than impersonal cause.
moves.warrant: A timeless impersonal cause possessing sufficient conditions would produce its effect automatically and therefore yield an infinitely old universe.
moves.inference: A personal cause can choose to create at a finite point, explaining a universe with a beginning.

sections.rationale: The selected rows separately cover the initial burden, openness to observation, the scientism reply, and the closing rule favoring investigated natural explanations.
The fourth pro row is required because the opening distinction, full grounding case, audience clarification, and closing synthesis are independently assessable in different live contexts.
The fourth con row is required because category scope, divine regress, fine-tuning alternative, and the closing nothing-from-nothing reversal target distinct inferential steps.

The initial divine-self-foreknowledge case, Slick’s naturalism redirect, Barker’s scope clarification, the human-freedom audience answer, and Barker’s own-actions rejoinder form distinct moves without exceeding four rows per side.

The fourth con row is required because Bible reliability, believer disagreement, the reply to divine-nature morality, and the rival-experience comparison test different forms of revelatory or divine authority.

The fourth pro row is required to preserve objective grounding, intrinsic-value restatement, the costly-altruism challenge, and the later justification challenge; con rows separately state harm grounding, evolutionary altruism, and practical guidance.

The fourth con row is required because public prayer evidence, general suffering, the explicitly limited failed-prayer conclusion, and the final studies/compassion answer are independently assessable.
